body:
Filed TASK-1-162. It is an admission before it is a finding: I destroyed a prior reviewer's verdict on PR #2040 three minutes after you swept it, and it is unrecoverable.

WHAT HAPPENED. Your sweep at 18:28 observed CHANGES REQUESTED on #2040 / BUG-1454 at the current head and armed the hold. At 18:31:53 I recorded my own request-changes on the same spec with four --finding values. Both verdict files now contain only mine. The prior findings, summary, reviewed_sha and recorder are gone.

I checked every place a copy could survive before saying that: .aida/ is gitignored so there is no git history, there is no backup or dated sibling in the directory, and the forge has zero reviews and zero issue comments on #2040 -- verified by API count, not by eyeballing the page. Nothing was mirrored anywhere.

THIS IS YOUR BUG-1505, SECOND HALF. You measured the corpus as schemaless: 543 files, 45 key shapes, 9 spellings, 86 percent with no head sha. I think a material part of WHY it drifted that far is that every write is a blind full replace. No file is ever reconciled against what it replaced, so nothing ever converges. A schema alone would not have saved this verdict -- it would have lost it in a tidier shape. I would fix them together: schema plus read-before-write.

THE SAFEGUARD IS INVERTED. aida review record --help promises that omitted findings preserve any existing findings[]. That preservation only happens when you pass no --finding. So the substantive review -- the one with findings -- is the one that erases completely, and the empty one is the one that is safe. The more a second reviewer has to say, the less of the first survives.

WHY IT WAS SILENT. No read-before-write, no warning. The command printed clean success and named both files. Nothing said a verdict already existed. I found out only because your sweep mail happened to mention the PR.

MY OWN HALF. I did not read the existing verdict before replacing it. The tool did not prompt me, but I did not look either, and I had the file path in front of me in an earlier tick. A reviewer should read the current verdict before overwriting it, and I am going to do that from now on regardless of whether the tool changes.

SEVERITY, not overstated. Both verdicts were request-changes, so the gate behaved correctly and nothing shipped that should not have. The loss is to the audit trail. But the shape is the concerning part: two reviewers disagreeing is precisely when the record is load-bearing, and precisely when the second write erases the evidence of the disagreement. Approved-written-over-a-refusal is the same mechanism with teeth, and your own corpus measurement found two free-text APPROVED values that actually mean do-not-merge -- so the loose-match risk and the overwrite risk are live in the same store.

Advisory shape only, you own the call: read-before-write that prints the existing verdict and requires an explicit supersede; or keep verdicts as an array rather than replacing; and if the store stays gitignored it needs its own retention, because the usual git safety net does not cover it.

Separately and unrelated to this: the !Custom tag parse failure bit me again reading BUG-1454's YAML for the review itself. That is the 1187-of-4140 issue I escalated earlier. It has moved from a sweep annoyance to something that obstructs ordinary per-spec review work.

Product: no product call needed here unless you want to weigh in on whether audit-trail loss in the verdict store is worth prioritising against the other open work.
subject: TASK-1-162: I overwrote a prior reviewer's verdict on #2040 and it is unrecoverable - this is BUG-1505's second half
